Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I will use the KNN classification technique in order to predict a team's tournament result. The reason for choosing this method is that my outcome variable tourney_finish has more than one category. Thus, I want to classify a team depending on its seed, conference wins, and conference win rate. However, the KNN algorithm may produce incorrect predictions since there might be fewer teams in some tournament result categories. Besides, scaling will be necessary because my predictors have different ranges. KNN is also sensitive to the choice of the number of neighbors, which may affect the model's performance.

To begin with, I will remove rows with missing values and split the data into training and testing samples. 75% of the samples will go for training while 25% will go for testing. I will split the data prior to preprocessing to prevent data leakage. I will use the training data to train the model and set the number of neighbors to 5. Then, I will test the model using the testing samples. I will not use a separate validation set or cross-validation in this analysis.

I will calculate the accuracy and the confusion matrix in order to evaluate the quality of my predictions. The accuracy score is going to show the proportion of correct predictions made by the algorithm. At the same time, the confusion matrix will show which results were predicted correctly or incorrectly for each category. Since some tournament results have fewer teams than others, accuracy alone may not fully show how well the model predicts less common results. Therefore, the confusion matrix will also help me understand the model's performance across different categories.

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [25]:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

# Select the variables needed for the analysis
knn_data <- womens_march_madness_tidy |>
  select(seed, conf_wins, conf_wins_pct, tourney_finish) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(tourney_finish = as_factor(tourney_finish))

# Set the random seed
set.seed(123)

# Split the data into training and testing sets
data_split <- initial_split(knn_data, prop = 0.75,
                            strata = tourney_finish)

# Create training and testing sets
training_data <- training(data_split)
testing_data <- testing(data_split)

# Scale and center the predictor variables
knn_recipe <- recipe(tourney_finish ~ seed + conf_wins +
                       conf_wins_pct,
                     data = training_data) |>
  step_scale(all_predictors()) |>
  step_center(all_predictors())

# Create a KNN classification model with 5 neighbors
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular",
                             neighbors = 5) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Combine the recipe and model into a workflow
knn_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(knn_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec)

# Train the model using the training data
knn_fit <- fit(knn_workflow, data = training_data)

# Predict tournament results using the testing data
knn_predictions <- predict(knn_fit, testing_data) |>
  bind_cols(testing_data)

# Calculate the accuracy
knn_accuracy <- knn_predictions |>
  metrics(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class) |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy")

knn_accuracy

# Create the confusion matrix
knn_confusion <- knn_predictions |>
  conf_mat(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class)

knn_confusion

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

My research question was whether a team's seed, conference wins, and conference win rate could help predict its final result in the NCAA Women's Basketball Tournament. I used a KNN classification model with 5 neighbors to make predictions. The model achieved an accuracy of 53.05% on the testing data. The confusion matrix showed that the model predicted first-round losses better than other results, with 198 correct predictions. However, it had more difficulty predicting results such as top 4 losses and championships. Overall, the results suggest that these three variables can provide some information about a team's tournament performance, but they are not enough to make highly accurate predictions.

During the analysis, I removed rows with missing values and scaled the predictor variables because KNN uses distances to compare teams. I also divided the data into training and testing sets to evaluate the model on data it had not used for training. I did not need to change my original analysis plan because the KNN method and the three predictors were suitable for my research question. I expected teams with better seeds and stronger conference records to have better tournament results, so I thought these variables would help with prediction. However, I was surprised that the model's accuracy was only 53.05%. One possible reason is that some tournament results have fewer teams than others, making them harder to predict. These findings show that predicting tournament results is not simple and that other factors may also be important. In the future, I could test different numbers of neighbors, compare KNN with other classification methods, or include more variables, such as regular-season wins and losses, to see if prediction accuracy improves.
